text: ServiceNow's Client Scripts fire at three distinct moments, and each one exists for a different job. This lesson walks through all three, and focuses on the one that actually has teeth: the script that can stop a bad record from saving at all.

onLoad runs once, right after the form finishes loading - good for setting initial field states. onChange runs every time one specific watched field's value changes, while the user is still editing. onSubmit runs when the user clicks save, before the record actually saves - and it's the only one of the three whose return value matters.

An onChange script receives real, useful parameters: oldValue, what the field held before; newValue, what it holds now; and isLoading, true while the form is still loading. That isLoading check matters - without it, this logic would also fire once while the form first loads, since the field technically changes from nothing to its stored value. Here, when the watched field becomes the value one, justification becomes mandatory; otherwise it doesn't.

onSubmit is different in one critical way: returning false from it blocks the save entirely. The record stays open, unsaved, exactly as the user left it. Here, when priority is one - meaning Critical - and justification is blank, an error message appears and the function returns false. Return true, or return nothing, and the save proceeds normally.

The strongest validation combines both. onChange gives the user immediate, friendly feedback as they type - a reminder they can still ignore. onSubmit is the final, unskippable backstop, enforcing the same rule at the moment of saving, because a user can always try to save anyway. And one more real behavior worth knowing: if a form has multiple onSubmit scripts, every one of them runs, and a single false from any of them is enough to block the save.

You now know all three Client Script types, and that only onSubmit's return value can stop a save. Next up: what happens when that validation needs server data through GlideAjax - because GlideAjax is asynchronous, and a naive return false can't actually wait for its callback to finish.
